description_full: Loews Corporation, through its subsidiaries, provides commercial property and casualty insurance in the United States and internationally. The company offers specialty insurance products, such as management and professional liability and other coverage products; surety and fidelity bonds; professional liability coverages and risk management services to various professional firms, including architects, real estate agents, and accounting and law firms; standard and excess property, marine and boiler, machinery coverages, workers' compensation, general and product liability, commercial auto, umbrella, excess and surplus coverages, specialized loss-sensitive insurance programs, total risk management services relating to claim and information services; directors and officers, errors and omissions, employment practices, fiduciary, fidelity, and cyber coverages, as well as for small and mid-size firms, public and privately held firms, and not-for-profit organizations; and insurance products to serve the health care industry, including professional and general liability, as well as associated casualty coverage to aging services, allied medical facilities, dentists, physicians, nurses, and other medical practitioners. It also provides warranty and alternative risk, and run-off long-term care insurance products; ethane supply and transportation services for petrochemical customers, as well as transports and stores natural gas and natural gas liquids; operates a chain of hotels; develops, manufactures, and markets a range of extrusion blow-molded and injection molded plastic containers; and manufactures commodities and differentiated plastic resins. The company markets its insurance products and services through a network of retail and wholesale brokers, independent agents, brokers, and managing general underwriters. Loews Corporation was incorporated in 1969 and is headquartered in New York, New York.
ceo_bio: Mr. Benjamin J. Tisch | CEO, President & Director | Age 42 | Compensation: $3.8M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 13K people. Revenue per employee of $1.4M ranks in the top quartile among Financial Services peers. Each employee generates $206K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $3K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (8/10).
financial_summary: Loews Corporation is a large-cap financial services business with a $22.6B market cap on $18.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $2.7B in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.97× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.9× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 5.2×.

Shareholder yield of 3.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 20% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.8) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Operating margins 17% below sector median — a cost disadvantage the moat cannot hide
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Priced near or above estimated fair value, so the margin of safety has been bid away
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are net sellers (75% sell ratio, net $27.0M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Fintech disintermediation — neobanks, embedded finance, and blockchain rails are unbundling the fee streams that traditional banks took for granted.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

sector_tailwinds: 39 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 12% operating margin trails the Financial Services median (29%) by 17pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.48x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.5% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 514 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 8% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 16% and a beta of 0.55, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.00 vs 5y 0.51), so read it loosely.
About $83.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 48% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 64% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $103 (margin of safety -9%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 10%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $64.41 to $164 (P10-P90).
Multiples send mixed signals against Financial Services peers: cheaper on P/FCF 8.4 vs 13.0, richer on P/E 15.5 vs 12.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 9% above its 10-year median.
The price implies 6.4% annual cash-flow growth.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.83).
It converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 9% return on equity.
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.5% over 3 years, 8.0% over 5 years and 3.2% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.27 (orders outpacing sales) and a backlog worth 1.3x annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 3.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 22, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 20.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 62%.
Insider trading is two-way: 2 purchases and 6 sales over the past year, net $27.0M sold.
It returns 3.8% a year to shareholders (3.6% in buybacks and 0.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 5.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, though it has been cut 5.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 13,100 employees, each generates about $1.4M of revenue, 2.8x the Financial Services median.
That works out to $206K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.8M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
